651.quote_or_event: “Wilt thou not cease to long for a family? How long wilt thou live in sorrow saying, It is for children? O my heart! there is no advantage that accrues to the soul except the good thou doest, though it be but little.”
651.explanation: The Naladiyar's chapter on the fear of misconduct says that no support from family or dependants profits the soul; only the good one does oneself, however small, brings real gain.
651.tie_back: Valluvar ranks the goodness of one's own deeds above the goodness of one's supporters; the Naladiyar likewise sets aside what others can do for us and counts only one's own good action.
651.source: Naladiyar, ch. 13 'The fear of misconduct', stanza 10 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
651._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. A Tamil Jain text, not canonical scripture. The contrast between others and one's own good deeds matches, but the stanza speaks of family, not allies, and of the soul's gain rather than every worldly good.

652.quote_or_event: “An intelligent man who has learned (the sacred texts) takes his duties upon himself, and he becomes renowned in the world; as the earth is the dwelling of all beings, so he will be a dwelling of all duties.”
652.explanation: The lecture on discipline presents renown as the natural result of taking up one's duties fully and rightly.
652.tie_back: The kural requires a deed to bring both good name and real good; the Jain verse joins renown to faithful performance of duty in the same way.
652.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.45 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
652._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (footnote marker removed). Next-best match only: Jainism treats fame as a by-product, never a test of action, and elsewhere (Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.19) tells the monk not to indulge his desire for fame, so the kural's fame-and-good test has no direct Jain parallel.

653.quote_or_event: “His knowledge will be honoured, his doubts will be removed, he will gladden the heart of his teacher by his good acts; kept in safety by the performance of austerities and by meditation, being as it were a great light, he will keep the five vows.”
653.explanation: The disciple who rises through good conduct is pictured as a great light, his standing secured by austerity, meditation and keeping the vows.
653.tie_back: The kural tells those who mean to rise higher to avoid any deed that dims their radiance; the Jain verse shows the other side, the light that pure conduct and kept vows make shine.
653.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.47 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
653._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The light image and the link between conduct and rising match, but the verse states the positive case only and has no explicit warning against deeds that dim one's name.

654.quote_or_event: “Though overcome by thirst, he should drink no cold water, restrained by shame and aversion (from forbidden things); he should try to get distilled water.”
654.explanation: Among the hardships a monk must bear, the Uttaradhyayana says that even when tormented by thirst he must not do what is forbidden, held back by shame and aversion.
654.tie_back: Valluvar says people of steady vision will not do shameful deeds even in deep distress; the Jain monk likewise holds to his rule under thirst, restrained by the same sense of shame.
654.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
654._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (footnote marker removed). Strong thematic fit on keeping one's standard under distress, though the forbidden act here is a monastic rule (unboiled water, which contains life), not a disgraceful political act.

655.quote_or_event: “He should not be angry with them nor do them any harm, nor say a single hard word to them, but he should promise not to commit the same sin again; for this is better than to do wrong.”
655.explanation: When a monk is corrected for a fault, the Sutrakritanga tells him to accept it calmly and promise not to commit the same sin again.
655.tie_back: The kural says to avoid deeds one will regret and, if one has done one, not to do the like again; the Jain verse makes exactly that promise of non-repetition the right response to a fault.
655.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
655._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Close match to the modern reading of the second line (not repeating the fault); it does not support the older Parimelazhagar reading about not grieving uselessly.

656.quote_or_event: “'Mother, father, daughter-in-law, brother, wife, and sons will not be able to help me, when I suffer for my own deeds.'”
656.explanation: Jainism teaches that each soul bears the fruit of its own karma alone, and no relative, not even a mother, can share or lift that burden.
656.tie_back: The kural forbids deeds the wise condemn even to relieve a starving mother; the Jain verse gives a reason in its own terms, since the doer alone will suffer for the wrong and the mother cannot help him then.
656.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com); the verse recurs at Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.9.5
656._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (footnote marker removed). Partial fit: the verse is about the limits of family help in karmic retribution and does not itself pose the dilemma of a hungry mother.

657.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.”
657.explanation: Mahavira warns that wealth won by evil deeds does not last, and that its owners end up caught in the snares of their own passions.
657.tie_back: The kural rates the poverty of the good above wealth won through disgrace; the Jain verse explains why such wealth is no prize, since it is lost and leaves its owner bound.
657.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
657._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong on the worthlessness of ill-gotten wealth; the kural's explicit comparison with the poverty of the good is not stated.

658.quote_or_event: “As the burglar caught in the breach of the wall perishes by the work the sinner himself had executed, thus people in this life and the next cannot escape the effect of their own actions.”
658.explanation: The commentator Devendra explains the image: a burglar who had dug his way through a wall is crushed when the wall above the breach comes down, killed by the very work he had completed.
658.tie_back: Valluvar says forbidden deeds bring suffering even when they succeed; the burglar's finished breach, which becomes his death, is a vivid picture of exactly that.
658.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.3, with Jacobi's note citing Devendra (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
658._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (footnote marker removed). Close match, including suffering in this life and the next; the kural's mention of deeds condemned by the wise is implied rather than stated.

659.quote_or_event: “Like as when the glittering spear that he cast is caught by his enemy's hand, the theif's courage is destroyed, so since the gains of sin follow after and destroy the acquirer of these gains in two births, it is good to leave the ignorant altogether.”
659.explanation: The Naladiyar teaches that sinful gains turn back on the one who acquired them, like a spear caught and turned by the enemy, and ruin him in this birth and the next.
659.tie_back: The kural says what is taken by making others weep will leave the taker weeping; the Naladiyar's spear that comes back on the thrower shows the same return of wrongful gain on its owner.
659.source: Naladiyar, ch. 13 'The fear of misconduct', stanza 9 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
659._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org; the translation's misspelling 'theif's' is kept as printed. A Tamil Jain text, not canonical scripture; it matches the first line of the kural but not the second, on fairly gained wealth bearing fruit later.

660.quote_or_event: “Wealth will not protect a careless man in this world and the next. Though he had seen the right way, he does not see it, even as one in the dark whose lamp has suddenly been put out.”
660.explanation: Mahavira teaches that wealth gives no real protection, in this life or the next, to one who has strayed from right conduct.
660.tie_back: The kural says that trying to secure oneself with wealth gained by deceit is like keeping water in an unfired clay pot; the Jain verse likewise denies that wealth can be relied on for protection.
660.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
660._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It shares the point that wealth cannot protect, but it speaks of carelessness rather than deceit, and it has no image like the unfired pot.
